newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.S. wants Kinshasa to avoid bloodshed and chaos.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wants Kinshasa to avoid bloodshed and chaos.

text.p: U.S. envoy Bill Richardson said on Monday he was pushing for a "soft landing" without bloodshed by Zairean rebels when they enter the capital Kinshasa.

"The objective of my urgent mission is to prepare a soft landing for Mr Kabila's rebels when they reach Kinshasa, a landing that avoids bloodshed and chaos," Richardson told a news conference after talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
Richardson brought Kabila what a U.S. dipolomat said was an urgent message from President Bill Clinton.

Kabila told his own news conference earlier: "If Mobutu hands over power before we enter Kinshasa, I will guarantee his safety and that of his biological family. But if he does not, we will have to chase him away in humiliation."
"I once again appeal to Mobutu to hand over power peacefully to me but if he does not do so my forces are ready to enter Kinshasa in the next two to three days," Kabila said.

Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said he met Rwandan military strongman Major-General Paul Kagame on Monday before seeing Kabila and would next see Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni who is visiting Botswana.

Rwanda and Uganda are two key supporters of the Tutsi-dominated rebels led by Kabila, who said on Monday his forces were ready to enter Kinshasa within two or three days and were less than 60 km (35 miles) from its international airport.
"President Museveni and General Kagame are key players on the scene here. We would like to make Kabila's entry as peaceful as possible. We want a soft landing followed by elections," Richardson said.
He later left rebel headquarters at Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city, for Botswana.

Troops from the United States, the former colonial power Belgium, France and Britain are waiting in Congo, across the river from Kinshasa, to evacuate Western nationals from the teeming capital of five million in the event of trouble.
Kabila met ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko on a South African navy ship on Sunday. They disagreed on arrangements for Mobutu to step down but agreed to meet again within eight to 10 days.
Mobutu wants to hand over power to some transitional body while Kabila wants to take over full control immediately.
The inconclusive talks on Sunday left many in Kinshasa feeling frustrated. Some people said Mobutu spoilt the party by refusing to step down, others feared what might happen next.
But with rebels advancing down the road to Kinshasa, markets operated normally and there was no sign of new military checkpoints in the centre of the city of five million people.

The rebels, seven months into a military offensive from the east, control three quarters of the country. The Zairean army has put up minimal resistance and Mobutu's foreign friends have largely abandoned him.
In Kisangani in northeast Zaire, rebels packed hundreds of Rwandan refugees on trucks on Monday and dropped them off metres from corpses of refugees killed in a train stampede on Sunday.
U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) officials received no notice of the convoy's arrival and again criticised rebel authorities for a lack of cooperation in the repatriation of Hutu refugees from Zaire.
"This is simply ridiculous," said a senior aid official. "You would have thought they would have learned a lesson."

UNHCR officials said 91 refugees were crushed to death and 48 injured on Sunday's train from Biaro, 41 km (25 miles) south of Kisangani, and ordered a suspension of railway evacuations to Kisangani for refugees to join an airlift home.
Some U.N. officials, who declined to be identified, said UNHCR should share some blame with the rebels for Sunday's deaths because both were in too much of a rush to move out the refugees.
The Rwandan Hutu refugees looked shocked on Monday on seeing a pile of corpses near the spot where they were dropped off.
